analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from using shared software services that pool rent data to coordinate rental prices.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban rent-fixing software was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since November 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it illegal for a company to gather rent and vacancy data from many landlords and use it to recommend what each should charge — the model of widely used revenue-management software. Using such a service would automatically violate antitrust law, with enforcement by the FTC, the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and private tenants, who could recover triple damages and could not be forced into arbitration. The bill was introduced in November 2025 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in markets where landlords use shared pricing software would benefit if coordinated rent increases are driven down by competition; tenants who paid inflated rents could recover triple damages in court and could not be forced into arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a per se antitrust violation for landlords to hire a 'coordinator' that collects rent data from multiple owners and recommends prices, renewal terms, or occupancy levels.

Tenants who were overcharged can sue for three times their damages plus attorney fees, and they can invalidate pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers that would otherwise push their claims into private arbitration.
It eases pleading standards in related Sherman Act cases so that rent collusion complaints cannot be dismissed just because landlords might have acted independently.
The FTC, the Justice Department, and every state attorney general can enforce the ban, and state laws providing stronger protections are preserved.

analysis.who_pays: Revenue-management software companies would lose their core market, and large landlords would lose a pricing tool and face treble-damage lawsuits; some coordination costs of pricing individually fall back on landlords.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rent-pricing software firms and large landlords

drawbacks.text: The bill bans a wide range of pricing-software services, not just one company: any firm that collects rent data from multiple landlords and recommends prices is unlawful, which landlords and software firms argue could sweep in ordinary property-management and market-reporting tools.
Because coordination is a per se violation, landlords using shared pricing tools would have no defense that their prices were reasonable or that the software genuinely improved efficiency.
Enforcement depends on litigation: tenants must sue or regulators must act, and the bill does not directly cap or set rents, so relief arrives only after cases are won.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to renters would be substantial if overcharges are as widespread as enforcement actions suggest, and the per se standard plus treble damages make the ban enforceable by ordinary tenants and state AGs. The main costs fall on landlords and software firms, though some economists argue pricing software also helps small landlords price accurately and that the bill's broad definition of a 'coordinator' could sweep in ordinary property-management tools. Honest supporters would acknowledge the bill reaches beyond any one company, but its design mirrors what courts and enforcers have already treated as unlawful collusion.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in November 2025, and with no hearing or vote scheduled it will likely sit there until the Congress ends, as most bills do.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 19, 2025 and read twice, then referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — has been taken since referral.
It has 12 cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, with no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the pricing-software and large-landlord interests that the bill targets are better off, since no vote has occurred and the bill faces long odds in a Republican-held Senate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pricing software firms and large landlords, so far

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its ban on rent-price coordination.

for.name: 12 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 11 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents (including Welch, Klobuchar, Booker, Sanders)

against.name: Senate Republicans (55)
against.what_they_did: None has cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled Senate has taken no action to move it out of committee.

against.name: RealPage and major corporate landlords
against.role: Rent-pricing software provider and its landlord customers
against.what_they_did: The bill targets the revenue-management software model these firms use; they are defendants in federal antitrust litigation over algorithmic rent-setting and have opposed restrictions on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents, and no Republican has signed on, making this a party-line bill so far.

industries.note: The bill makes their core service — pooling rent data from many landlords and recommending prices — a per se Sherman Act violation, eliminating a major market. Tenants bear those software-driven rent increases today, so the loss aligns with the public's gain.
They would lose access to coordinated pricing tools that, under the bill's theory, let them push rents up in tandem; they would have to price units independently.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no hearing or markup scheduled and no Republican support. First-year bills of this kind rarely reach the floor, and with Republicans holding 55 Senate seats, its realistic path is to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless it is folded into a larger package.
